note: Every dinner here has a vegetarian base that the whole table eats. The omnivore block is a fork-in-the-road: one extra pan or tray, cooked alongside, so nobody makes two dinners.

recipes.title: Weeknight Lentil Bolognese
recipes.blurb: The sauce that converts people. Lentils, a soffritto cooked past the point most people stop, and tomato paste fried until it darkens — it tastes like it simmered all afternoon.
steps: Heat the oil in a dutch oven over medium. Add onion, carrot, celery and a pinch of salt. Cook 10-12 minutes, stirring now and then, until everything is soft and the onion is genuinely golden — not translucent, golden. This is the step that separates good sauce from flat sauce.
Add garlic, oregano, crushed fennel seed and pepper flakes. Cook 60 seconds until fragrant.
Push everything to one side, add the tomato paste to the bare pan, and let it fry undisturbed for 60-90 seconds until it turns brick red and smells sweet. Stir it in.

Add lentils, crushed tomatoes, broth, bay leaf, salt and pepper. Bring to a simmer, cover partway, and cook 30-35 minutes until the lentils are tender and the sauce is thick enough to hold a spoon track.
Meanwhile, cook the pasta in well-salted water. Reserve a cup of pasta water before draining.
Pull the bay leaf. Stir in the balsamic — this is the finishing move; it wakes the whole pot up. Taste and adjust.
Toss the drained pasta directly into the sauce with a splash of pasta water so it clings. Finish with torn basil and parmesan at the table.

omnivore.label: Add browned turkey
omnivore.note: Brown it in a separate skillet and add it to individual bowls, or stir it into half the pot. The sauce is built to work either way.
steps: Brown the turkey in a dry skillet over medium-high, breaking it up, 6-8 minutes. Season with a pinch of salt, pepper and a shake of fennel seed.
Ladle some of the finished lentil sauce into the skillet, stir, and serve that pan over the omnivores' pasta.

recipes.kidTweak: Blend one cup of the finished sauce smooth with an immersion blender and stir it back in if your kids object to visible vegetables. Serve their portion before you add pepper flakes.
recipes.restaurantTouch: Finish each bowl with a half teaspoon of good olive oil and a grating of parmesan at the table, not in the pot. The aroma hits before the first bite.
recipes.garden: Garden basil and paste tomatoes are what make this in August. Two Amish Paste plants will supply a winter of frozen sauce.
recipes.leftovers: Sauce keeps 5 days refrigerated, 3 months frozen. It is better on day two. Freeze in 2-cup portions flat in bags.
recipes.prepAhead: Make the sauce Sunday; Tuesday dinner is 12 minutes of boiling water.

recipes.title: Sheet-Pan Crispy Tofu and Broccoli, Sesame-Ginger Glaze
recipes.blurb: Cornstarch-dusted tofu that actually gets crisp in a home oven, broccoli with charred edges, and a glaze that goes on at the end so it never burns.

ingredients.prep: cut into florets, stems peeled and sliced

steps: Heat the oven to 425°F with both racks in the upper half. Press the tofu between paper towels under a heavy pan for 15 minutes while you start the rice.
Toss the tofu cubes with cornstarch until every face is chalky-dry, then with the canola oil. Spread on a sheet pan with space between cubes — crowding steams them.
Toss the broccoli with olive oil and a pinch of salt on the second pan, cut sides down.
Roast both 22-25 minutes, flipping the tofu once at 15 minutes. The broccoli should have real char on the edges.
Whisk soy sauce, maple, rice vinegar, ginger, garlic, sesame oil and pepper flakes in a large bowl.
Tip the hot tofu and broccoli straight into the bowl and toss — the residual heat makes the glaze grab. Serve over brown rice with scallions.

omnivore.label: Add glazed chicken thighs
omnivore.note: Same glaze, same oven, third pan. Add it 5 minutes after the vegetables go in.
steps: Toss the chicken with 1 tbsp cornstarch and a teaspoon of oil, spread on a third pan, and roast 18-20 minutes at 425°F until 165°F internal.
Toss it in a spoonful of the glaze separately so the vegetarian batch stays meat-free.

recipes.kidTweak: Pull a handful of plain crispy tofu cubes and plain broccoli before glazing. Serve with a small bowl of glaze for dipping — dipping wins where sauced-on loses.
recipes.restaurantTouch: The cornstarch coating is the whole trick, and it is what every good Chinese-American kitchen does. Do not skip pressing.
recipes.garden: Broccoli side shoots keep producing for weeks after you cut the main head, and they roast better than the crown.
recipes.leftovers: Tofu softens overnight. Re-crisp in a hot dry skillet for 3 minutes; do not microwave.

recipes.title: Chickpea Shakshuka
recipes.blurb: Eggs poached in a smoky pepper-tomato sauce with chickpeas for staying power. Twenty-five minutes, one skillet, and it feels like a restaurant brunch at 6pm.
steps: Heat oil over medium in a 12-inch skillet. Cook onion and pepper 8 minutes until soft and starting to color.
Add garlic, cumin, smoked paprika and pepper flakes; 45 seconds. Add tomato paste and fry it 60 seconds until darkened.
Add crushed tomatoes, chickpeas and salt. Simmer 8-10 minutes until thick enough that a spoon leaves a trail.
Make six wells with the back of a spoon and crack an egg into each. Season the eggs. Cover and cook 6-8 minutes — whites set, yolks still loose.
Scatter feta and parsley over the top. Bring the skillet to the table with warm pita and let everyone tear in.

omnivore.label: Add merguez-style turkey
omnivore.note: Brown first, in the same pan, then build the sauce on top — or keep it separate in a small skillet if the cook is vegetarian.
steps: Brown the turkey with an extra teaspoon each of cumin and smoked paprika in a small skillet, 7 minutes.
Spoon it over the omnivores' half of the skillet before you crack in the eggs.

recipes.kidTweak: Kids who won't eat a runny yolk get theirs cooked 3 minutes longer, or scrambled into the sauce on their side of the pan.
recipes.restaurantTouch: A spoonful of plain Greek yogurt swirled on top just before serving, and a hard squeeze of lemon.
recipes.garden: Late-summer peppers and tomatoes from the garden turn this into something else entirely.
recipes.leftovers: The sauce base keeps 4 days without eggs. Reheat and poach fresh eggs to order.

recipes.title: Smoky Black Bean and Sweet Potato Tacos
recipes.blurb: Caramelized sweet potato, smoky beans, crunchy slaw, charred corn tortillas. The kind of taco night where nobody notices there's no meat.
steps: Heat oven to 425°F. Toss sweet potato with 1 tbsp oil, half the cumin, half the smoked paprika, chili powder and salt. Roast 25 minutes, tossing once, until the edges are dark and sweet.
Meanwhile toss the shredded cabbage with the juice of one lime and a pinch of salt. Let it sit — it softens and sharpens while everything else cooks.

Warm the remaining oil in a skillet, add garlic and the rest of the spices for 30 seconds, then the black beans and 2 tbsp water. Smash about a third of the beans against the pan so they go creamy. Cook 5 minutes.
Thin the yogurt with lime juice and a pinch of salt to make a drizzle.
Char the tortillas directly over a gas burner or in a dry skillet, 20 seconds a side, and stack them in a towel to steam.
Build: beans, sweet potato, slaw, avocado, cilantro, jalapeño, lime crema.

omnivore.label: Add chili-lime shrimp or chicken
omnivore.note: Three minutes in a hot skillet while the tortillas warm.
steps: Toss shrimp with a teaspoon of oil, a pinch of chili powder and salt.
Sear in a hot skillet 90 seconds a side until just opaque. Squeeze lime over and serve on the side.

recipes.kidTweak: Deconstruct it: a bowl of plain roasted sweet potato, a bowl of beans, cheese, and warm tortillas. Kids assemble their own, which is the entire reason they eat it.
recipes.restaurantTouch: Char the tortillas over open flame. It takes 40 seconds and it is the single biggest upgrade in home taco night.
recipes.garden: Cilantro and jalapeños are two of the easiest things to grow here, and both peak exactly when you want tacos.
recipes.leftovers: Filling keeps 4 days. It becomes a burrito bowl over rice with zero extra work.

recipes.title: 25-Minute Red Lentil Dal
recipes.blurb: Red lentils collapse into something creamy with no cream at all. Finished with a sizzling spice oil poured over at the table.

ingredients.prep: rinsed until the water runs clear

steps: Start the rice. Then heat canola oil in a saucepan over medium, cook the onion 6 minutes, add garlic and ginger for 1 minute.
Add turmeric, cumin and coriander; stir 30 seconds until they smell toasty.
Add lentils, broth, tomatoes and salt. Simmer uncovered 18-20 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the lentils have completely broken down.
Stir in coconut milk and spinach; cook 2 minutes until the spinach wilts. Squeeze in lime juice.
The tarka: heat olive oil in a small skillet until shimmering, add pepper flakes and garam masala, count to ten, and pour it sizzling over the pot. Stir once.
Serve over jasmine rice with cilantro.

omnivore.label: Add roasted chicken thighs
omnivore.note: Rub with the same spice mix and roast while the dal simmers.
steps: Rub thighs with 1 tsp each cumin and turmeric, a pinch of salt and a teaspoon of oil.
Roast at 425°F for 20-22 minutes. Slice and lay over the omnivores' bowls.

recipes.kidTweak: Hold the tarka off the kids' bowls — it carries all the heat. Dal over rice with a spoon of yogurt is about as kid-safe as dinner gets.
recipes.restaurantTouch: The sizzling spice oil poured at the table is theater, and it takes 60 seconds. Do it in front of everyone.
recipes.garden: Nothing to grow here except cilantro, which bolts in July heat — sow a new short row every three weeks.
recipes.leftovers: Thickens overnight into something closer to a spread. Loosen with water. Freezes 3 months.

recipes.title: Mushroom Farro "Risotto"
recipes.blurb: All the comfort of risotto with a chewy whole grain and none of the standing-and-stirring. Deeply savory from properly browned mushrooms.
steps: Heat 2 tbsp oil in a wide skillet over medium-high until it shimmers. Add the mushrooms in a single layer and — this is the important part — do not touch them or salt them for 4 minutes. Let them brown, then toss and brown 4 more minutes. Season, remove, set aside.
Lower the heat to medium. Add the last tablespoon of oil, the shallots and a pinch of salt; cook 3 minutes. Add garlic and thyme, 45 seconds.
Add farro and toast it in the fat for 2 minutes until it smells nutty.
Pour in the wine and let it cook away completely, scraping the bottom.
Add warm broth a cup at a time, stirring occasionally and adding more as it absorbs — about 30 minutes total. Farro is forgiving; it does not need constant attention like arborio.

When the grains are tender with a little chew, stir the mushrooms back in with parmesan, butter and lemon zest. It should be loose enough to spread slowly on the plate. Finish with parsley and a lot of black pepper.

omnivore.label: Add seared steak or a fried egg
omnivore.note: Sliced sirloin over the top turns this into a restaurant entrée; a crispy fried egg does the same job for less money.
steps: Salt the steak 40 minutes ahead if you can. Sear in a very hot cast iron skillet, 3-4 minutes a side for medium-rare.
Rest 8 minutes, slice thin against the grain, and fan it over the omnivores' plates.

recipes.kidTweak: Most kids will eat the farro plain with parmesan. Set a portion aside before the mushrooms go back in.
recipes.restaurantTouch: The lemon zest at the end is what makes people ask what's in it. Do not substitute juice — the oil in the zest is the point.
recipes.garden: Thyme is a perennial here; one plant survives Ohio winters and you snip from it for years.
recipes.leftovers: Press cold leftovers into patties and pan-fry in olive oil for arancini-adjacent lunch.

recipes.title: Tuscan White Bean and Kale Soup
recipes.blurb: Half the beans blended into the broth makes it creamy without a drop of cream. This is the pot to make on the first cold Sunday in October.

ingredients.prep: toasted, rubbed with a cut garlic clove

steps: Cook onion, carrot and celery in the oil over medium for 10 minutes with a pinch of salt until soft and sweet.
Add garlic, rosemary and pepper flakes for a minute, then the tomato paste; fry it 60 seconds until it darkens.
Add one can of beans, the tomatoes, broth, bay leaf and salt. Simmer 15 minutes.
Pull the bay leaf. Blend directly in the pot with an immersion blender for about 10 seconds — just enough to thicken the broth while leaving plenty of texture.
Add the second can of beans and the kale. Simmer 8 minutes until the kale is tender but still green.
Finish with lemon juice. Serve over garlic-rubbed toast with parmesan.

omnivore.label: Add Italian chicken sausage
omnivore.note: One link, browned and sliced, seasons six bowls. Treat it as a seasoning, not the protein — one link carries about 600 mg of sodium.
steps: Brown the sausage whole in a dry skillet, 8 minutes, then slice into coins.
Add to individual bowls so the pot stays vegetarian.

recipes.kidTweak: Blend a full cup smooth for a kid who is suspicious of soup with things in it, and serve the toast on the side for dunking.
recipes.restaurantTouch: The garlic-rubbed toast under the soup instead of crackers on the side. Ten seconds of work, completely different dish.
recipes.garden: Lacinato kale is the last thing standing in an Ohio garden — pick it under snow in December and it will be sweeter than it was in September.
recipes.leftovers: Better on day two. Freezes 3 months; add the kale fresh when reheating if you want it bright green.

recipes.title: Pasta e Ceci
recipes.blurb: Roman pantry cooking: chickpeas, pasta, rosemary and a lot of olive oil, cooked in one pot until the starch turns the broth silky. Thirty minutes, seven dollars.
steps: Warm the oil, garlic, rosemary and pepper flakes together over medium — start them in cold oil so the garlic perfumes the fat instead of burning. 3 minutes.
Add tomato paste, fry 60 seconds. Add one can of chickpeas and mash them roughly with a wooden spoon.
Add the second can, the broth and salt. Simmer 10 minutes.
Add the dry pasta directly to the pot and cook, stirring often, until al dente — 9-11 minutes. The pasta starch is what makes the broth silky, so do not boil it separately.
Off heat, stir in parmesan and lemon juice, and let it sit 3 minutes to thicken. Finish with parsley and a hard pour of raw olive oil over each bowl.

omnivore.label: Add tuna or pancetta-style crisp
omnivore.note: A drained can of good tuna flaked into the omnivore bowls is traditional along the Italian coast and takes zero cooking.
steps: Flake the tuna over the omnivores' bowls with extra black pepper and lemon.

recipes.kidTweak: Use a fun small pasta shape and go light on the pepper flakes. Most kids treat this as 'bean soup with noodles' and eat two bowls.
recipes.restaurantTouch: Finishing oil poured raw over the bowl — a full teaspoon each. It smells like a trattoria and it is the healthiest fat in the kitchen.
recipes.garden: Rosemary in a pot by the door, dragged inside in November.
recipes.leftovers: The pasta drinks the broth overnight. Add half a cup of water when reheating.
recipes.source: ERRERLabs original, after the Roman classic

recipes.title: Charred Cauliflower Steaks with Romesco
recipes.blurb: Thick-cut cauliflower roasted until the edges go mahogany, over a smoky almond-pepper sauce that takes four minutes in a blender. This is the one to cook for company.

ingredients.prep: cut into 1-inch steaks through the core

steps: Heat oven to 450°F with a sheet pan inside. A preheated pan is what gives you a hard sear on the first side.
Brush the cauliflower steaks with 3 tbsp oil and season with half the smoked paprika, the cumin and salt. Scatter the chickpeas and any loose florets around them.
Lay everything on the screaming-hot pan and roast 25-30 minutes, flipping the steaks once at 18 minutes, until deeply browned at the edges.

Romesco: blend roasted peppers, almonds, garlic, tomato paste, vinegar, the rest of the smoked paprika and 2 tbsp oil with a pinch of salt until it is a coarse sauce, about 30 seconds. Taste — it should be bright and a little rough.
Cook the couscous per the package (5 minutes, off heat, covered).
Spread romesco on warm plates, set the cauliflower on top, scatter chickpeas and parsley. Serve couscous alongside.

omnivore.label: Add seared shrimp or lamb-spiced chicken
omnivore.note: Romesco was born to sit under seafood.
steps: Toss shrimp with a teaspoon of oil, smoked paprika and salt.
Sear 90 seconds a side in a hot skillet and lay over the omnivores' romesco.

recipes.kidTweak: Break the extra florets into 'cauliflower popcorn' and serve them plain with a small dish of romesco to dip.
recipes.restaurantTouch: Sauce on the plate, vegetable on the sauce — never the other way around. It is the whole difference between home plating and restaurant plating.
recipes.garden: Fall cauliflower transplanted August 1 heads up in October when the weather is on your side.
recipes.leftovers: Romesco keeps 5 days and turns eggs, sandwiches and roasted potatoes into something else. Make a double batch.

recipes.title: Garden Stir-Fry with Crisp Tofu
recipes.blurb: Whatever the garden or the crisper drawer is giving you, cooked hot and fast in a sauce built from four pantry bottles. Fifteen minutes once the prep is done.
steps: Prep everything and line it up by the stove before you turn on the heat. Stir-frying gives you no time to chop.
Whisk soy sauce, rice vinegar, maple syrup (or honey, if vegan is not a concern), sesame oil and 2 tbsp water with 1 tsp of the cornstarch. Set by the stove.
Toss the tofu with the remaining cornstarch. Heat 1 tbsp canola in a wok over high until it smokes lightly, add tofu in one layer and leave it alone 3 minutes. Toss, brown 3 more, remove.
Add the last tablespoon of oil. Carrots first, 90 seconds. Then peppers and snap peas, 2 minutes. Then bok choy, 1 minute — hard vegetables first, tender last.
Garlic and ginger, 30 seconds. Return tofu, pour in the sauce, and toss 60 seconds until it glosses everything.
Off heat, scallions. Serve over jasmine rice immediately.

omnivore.label: Add velveted chicken
omnivore.note: Cornstarch on the chicken too — the same trick that makes takeout chicken silky.
steps: Toss sliced chicken with 1 tbsp cornstarch and 1 tsp soy sauce; rest 10 minutes.
Sear in a separate hot skillet 4-5 minutes until cooked through, then toss with a spoonful of the sauce.

recipes.kidTweak: Kids usually want the components apart: crispy tofu, plain rice, raw snap peas on the side. That is still dinner.
recipes.restaurantTouch: Get the pan hotter than feels reasonable and do not crowd it. Restaurant stir-fry tastes different because of heat, not ingredients.
recipes.garden: This is the recipe that absorbs a garden glut — snap peas in June, beans in July, peppers in August, bok choy in October.
recipes.leftovers: Eat it the same night; stir-fried vegetables go limp. Leftover rice is tomorrow's fried rice.

recipes.title: Skillet Eggplant Parmesan
recipes.blurb: Roasted, not fried. Crisp panko goes on top at the end so it stays crunchy. All the comfort of the casserole with a third of the fat and half the dishes.
steps: Heat oven to 425°F. Salt the eggplant rounds and let them sit 15 minutes, then blot dry — this seasons them through and pulls the water that otherwise makes the dish soggy.
Brush both sides with 2 tbsp oil, spread on a sheet pan, and roast 25 minutes, flipping once, until browned and collapsed.
Toast the panko with the last tablespoon of oil in a dry skillet over medium, stirring, 3-4 minutes until golden. Tip it onto a plate — this is your crunch, and it goes on last.
In the same skillet, warm the marinara with the garlic and pepper flakes, 5 minutes.
Layer in the skillet: sauce, eggplant, mozzarella, repeat, finishing with sauce and parmesan. Bake 15 minutes until bubbling.
Scatter the toasted panko and torn basil over the top just before serving so it stays crisp.

omnivore.label: Add chicken cutlets
omnivore.note: Same treatment, separate pan: pound thin, panko, roast alongside the eggplant.
steps: Brush cutlets with olive oil, press into panko, roast at 425°F for 15-18 minutes on their own pan.
Top with sauce and cheese in the last 3 minutes.

recipes.kidTweak: Serve over pasta with extra sauce. The panko on top does most of the persuading.
recipes.restaurantTouch: Panko added after baking instead of before. Nobody does this at home and everybody notices.
recipes.garden: One eggplant plant produces more than a family can eat from August through frost.
recipes.leftovers: Reheats well at 350°F. Re-toast fresh panko for the top — 3 minutes and it tastes new.

recipes.title: Butternut and Chickpea Curry
recipes.blurb: Sweet squash, creamy chickpeas, and a coconut broth that tastes like it took an hour. It takes thirty-five minutes and one pot.
steps: Cook the onion in oil over medium 6 minutes. Add garlic and ginger, 1 minute.
Add the curry paste and fry it in the oil 90 seconds until it darkens and the kitchen smells like a restaurant. This is the step people skip and it is the whole flavor.
Add squash, chickpeas, coconut milk and broth. Simmer covered 20 minutes until the squash yields to a knife but still holds its shape.
Stir in spinach until wilted, 2 minutes. Finish with lime juice — taste, and add more; the acid is what makes coconut curry taste finished rather than heavy.
Serve over jasmine rice with cilantro and toasted pepitas.

omnivore.label: Add poached chicken or seared shrimp
omnivore.note: Poach chicken pieces directly in a ladle of the curry in a small pot for 10 minutes so it tastes like the same dish.
steps: Ladle 1.5 cups of the finished curry into a small pot, add the chicken, and simmer 10-12 minutes until cooked through. Serve that pot to the omnivores.

recipes.kidTweak: Curry paste brands vary wildly in heat. Start with 2 tbsp, taste after step 3, and add more for the adults at the end.
recipes.restaurantTouch: Toasted pepitas on top for crunch and a lime wedge on every plate.
recipes.garden: Butternut stores in a cool basement until February — one summer's harvest covers a winter of these.
recipes.leftovers: Freezes beautifully for 3 months. The squash gets softer; nobody minds.

recipes.title: Greek Quinoa Bowls with Whipped Feta
recipes.blurb: Everything cold and crunchy over warm quinoa, with a whipped feta that takes two minutes and tastes like a restaurant meze plate.
steps: Cook the quinoa in 2.5 cups water, 15 minutes, then rest covered 5 minutes off heat and fluff. Toss warm with 1 tbsp olive oil and 1 tbsp lemon juice so it absorbs the dressing.
Whipped feta: blend the feta with the yogurt and 1 tbsp lemon juice for 60 seconds until it is smooth and spreadable. Loosen with a spoon of water if needed.
Whisk the remaining lemon juice, 3 tbsp olive oil, oregano and black pepper into a dressing. No salt needed — the feta and olives bring plenty.
Toss cucumber, tomatoes, red onion, olives and chickpeas with half the dressing.
Build: a swipe of whipped feta on the bottom of each bowl, warm quinoa, romaine, the vegetable mix, the rest of the dressing, and dill over everything.

omnivore.label: Add oregano-lemon chicken
omnivore.note: Marinate in the morning, grill or roast in 20 minutes at dinner.
steps: Marinate chicken in 1 tbsp olive oil, 1 tbsp lemon juice, 1 tsp oregano, garlic and pepper for at least 20 minutes.
Grill or roast at 425°F for 18-20 minutes to 165°F, rest 5 minutes, slice.

recipes.kidTweak: Serve it as a plate, not a bowl — quinoa in one spot, cucumbers and tomatoes in another, feta dip with pita on the side. Kids who won't eat a mixed bowl will eat every component.
recipes.restaurantTouch: The whipped feta swiped across the bottom of the bowl instead of crumbled on top. It costs nothing and looks like a $19 lunch.
recipes.garden: Cucumbers, cherry tomatoes and dill all peak together in late July, which is exactly when you want this.
recipes.leftovers: Best meal-prep lunch in the collection. Keep dressing separate; assembled bowls hold 4 days.

recipes.title: Friday Night Garden Pizza
recipes.blurb: Store-bought whole wheat dough, a hot stone or steel, and whatever is ripe. Everyone builds their own half, which is the entire point.
equipment: pizza stone, steel, or inverted sheet pan
steps: Put the stone or steel on the top rack and heat the oven to its absolute maximum — 500-550°F — for a full 45 minutes. Home pizza fails on temperature, not technique.
Stretch the dough on a floured peel or parchment. Do not roll it; press from the center out with your fingertips and let gravity do the rest.
Sauce thinly — a scant half cup per pizza. Too much sauce is why home pizza goes soggy.
Top: cheese, cherry tomatoes, zucchini ribbons, garlic, a drizzle of oil. Let each kid build their own half.
Bake 7-9 minutes until the crust is blistered and the cheese is browning in spots.
Out of the oven: torn basil, and a handful of arugula tossed with lemon and oil piled in the center. The greens wilt just slightly against the hot crust.

omnivore.label: Add crumbled Italian chicken sausage
omnivore.note: Brown it first — raw sausage on a 9-minute pizza does not cook through.
steps: Squeeze the sausage out of its casing, brown it in a skillet 6 minutes, and scatter it over the omnivores' half before baking.

recipes.kidTweak: The whole recipe is the kid tweak. Give them their own dough ball, let them make it badly, and eat it anyway.
recipes.restaurantTouch: Dressed arugula piled on after baking. It turns a homemade pizza into something you would order.
recipes.garden: August: cherry tomatoes, zucchini and basil walk in from the yard and go straight on the dough.
recipes.leftovers: Reheat slices in a dry skillet over medium with a lid, 4 minutes. Crisp bottom, melted top, never soggy.

recipes.title: Summer Corn and Zucchini over Creamy Polenta
recipes.blurb: August on a plate. Sweet corn and blistered zucchini over soft polenta, with goat cheese melting into it.
steps: Bring broth and milk to a bare simmer with half the salt. Rain in the cornmeal while whisking constantly — lumps form in the first 30 seconds or not at all.
Cook on low 20-25 minutes, whisking every few minutes, until it is thick and no longer gritty. Off heat, stir in parmesan and butter.
Meanwhile heat a cast iron skillet over medium-high with the olive oil. Add zucchini cut-side down in one layer and leave it alone 4 minutes until it blisters.
Add corn, garlic and pepper flakes; 3 minutes. Add cherry tomatoes and cook 2 minutes just until they slump. Season, and finish with lemon juice.
Spoon polenta into wide bowls, pile the vegetables on top, and scatter goat cheese and basil so it melts into the heat.

omnivore.label: Add seared shrimp or sliced grilled chicken
omnivore.note: Shrimp cook in the same skillet in 3 minutes after the vegetables come out.
steps: Sear the shrimp in the same hot skillet, 90 seconds a side, and set them over the omnivores' bowls.

recipes.kidTweak: Polenta is essentially savory porridge and most kids love it. Serve theirs with corn and cheese only, vegetables alongside.
recipes.restaurantTouch: Wide shallow bowls, polenta spread with the back of a spoon rather than mounded, vegetables piled slightly off-center.
recipes.garden: This exists to solve the August zucchini problem. Local Ohio sweet corn from a roadside stand is worth the detour.
recipes.leftovers: Polenta sets solid in the fridge. Slice it into slabs and pan-fry in olive oil until crisp — a completely different, better dish.

recipes.title: Quinoa and Black Bean Stuffed Peppers
recipes.blurb: Make-ahead, freezer-friendly, and one of the few dinners that is genuinely as good reheated. Every pepper is a complete meal.
steps: Heat oven to 375°F. Cook quinoa in 2 cups water, 15 minutes, rest 5, fluff.
Cook onion in oil 6 minutes; add garlic and all the spices for 45 seconds until fragrant.
Stir in beans, corn, salsa and the cooked quinoa. Squeeze in the lime. Taste and adjust — season the filling properly now, because you cannot fix it later.
Arrange the pepper halves cut-side up in a baking dish, pack them full, and add a half inch of water to the dish. Cover tightly with foil.
Bake covered 30 minutes, uncover, top with cheese, and bake 10 more until the peppers are tender and the cheese browns.
Cilantro and a spoon of yogurt on top.

omnivore.label: Add ground turkey to half the filling
omnivore.note: Brown it separately, then stir it into half the filling before stuffing. Mark the omnivore peppers with a toothpick.
steps: Brown the turkey with a teaspoon of the spice mix, 7 minutes, and fold it into half the quinoa filling.

recipes.kidTweak: Skip the pepper entirely for a resistant kid and bake their filling in a small ramekin with cheese on top. Same dinner, no negotiation.
recipes.restaurantTouch: A quick pickle of thinly sliced red onion in lime juice and salt, made when you start cooking, scattered over at the end.
recipes.garden: Peppers ripen from green to red on the plant in September and the red ones are twice as sweet.
recipes.leftovers: Freeze stuffed and unbaked. Bake from frozen, covered, 50 minutes.

recipes.title: Miso Noodle Bowl with Bok Choy
recipes.blurb: A ten-minute broth that tastes like it simmered with bones. Miso goes in off the heat, which is the rule that makes or breaks it.
steps: Simmer broth with ginger and garlic for 10 minutes, then fish them out. Add shiitakes and simmer 5 more.
Cook the rice noodles separately per the package and rinse them — cooking them in the broth turns it cloudy and gluey.
Add tofu, bok choy and edamame to the broth; simmer 3 minutes until the greens are just tender.
Off the heat — genuinely off, not low — whisk the miso with a ladle of hot broth in a small bowl until smooth, then stir it back in. Boiling miso kills the flavor and the live cultures.
Add soy sauce and sesame oil. Taste; it should be savory and round.
Divide noodles into bowls, ladle broth and vegetables over, and top with scallions, pepper flakes and a soft-boiled egg half.

omnivore.label: Add shredded chicken
omnivore.note: Poach a breast right in the broth at the start, then shred it.
steps: Poach the chicken in the simmering broth for 15 minutes, remove, shred, and add to the omnivores' bowls. Note this makes the broth non-vegetarian, so do it in a separate small pot if the cook is vegetarian.

recipes.kidTweak: Serve deconstructed: noodles in the bowl, a little broth, edamame on the side. Most kids negotiate over the broth, not the noodles.
recipes.restaurantTouch: The soft-boiled egg: 6 minutes 30 seconds in boiling water, then ice water. Jammy yolk, every time.
recipes.garden: Bok choy grows in 45 days and tolerates the cold snaps that kill everything else in April.
recipes.leftovers: Store noodles and broth separately or you will find soup with no noodles and noodles with no soup.

recipes.title: Three-Bean Smoky Chili
recipes.blurb: A spoonful of cocoa and a lot of smoked paprika do what a pound of beef used to. Better on day two, and it feeds a crowd for under ten dollars.
steps: Cook onions and peppers in oil over medium-high 10 minutes until they take on color. Do not rush this — browned vegetables are the backbone of a meatless chili.
Add garlic and all the dry spices; stir 60 seconds. Add tomato paste and cocoa and fry 90 seconds until everything is dark and fragrant.
Add crushed tomatoes, all three cans of beans, broth and salt. Simmer uncovered 30 minutes, stirring occasionally.
Add corn in the last 5 minutes. Finish with the juice of both limes off the heat.
Set out yogurt, cheddar, cilantro and avocado and let everyone build their own bowl.

omnivore.label: Add browned ground turkey
omnivore.note: A half pound browned separately and stirred into half the pot covers four omnivore servings.
steps: Brown the turkey with 1 tsp chili powder and a pinch of salt, 8 minutes, and stir it into half the pot after step 3.

recipes.kidTweak: Chili powder brands vary. Use 1 tbsp for a kid-safe pot and put hot sauce on the table for the adults.
recipes.restaurantTouch: Lime juice off the heat at the end. Chili without acid tastes muddy, and almost nobody does this at home.
recipes.garden: Peppers and onions from the garden in September make this taste like a different recipe.
recipes.leftovers: Genuinely better on day two and three. Freezes 3 months. Leftover chili over a baked sweet potato is a whole second dinner.

recipes.title: Za'atar Sheet-Pan Chickpeas and Vegetables with Tahini
recipes.blurb: One pan, twenty-five minutes in the oven, and a lemon-tahini sauce that makes it feel composed rather than thrown together.
steps: Heat oven to 425°F. Dry the chickpeas thoroughly on a towel — wet chickpeas steam instead of crisping.
Toss cauliflower, carrots and onion with 2 tbsp oil, 1 tbsp za'atar, cumin and salt on one pan. Toss chickpeas with the remaining oil and za'atar on the second.
Roast both 25-30 minutes, stirring once. The chickpeas should rattle and the cauliflower should be brown at the tips.
Tahini sauce: whisk tahini, lemon juice, garlic and a pinch of salt. It will seize into a paste — keep whisking in cold water a tablespoon at a time until it turns pale and pourable.
Make the couscous: 1 cup couscous, 1.25 cups boiling water, covered, 5 minutes, fluff.
Pile everything over couscous, pour tahini over generously, and finish with parsley and pepitas.

omnivore.label: Add za'atar chicken thighs
omnivore.note: Third pan, same seasoning, same oven, 22 minutes.
steps: Rub thighs with oil and za'atar and roast at 425°F for 22-25 minutes to 165°F.

recipes.kidTweak: The crispy chickpeas are the sell. Give a kid a bowl of just those plus plain couscous and tahini for dipping.
recipes.restaurantTouch: Pour the tahini in a wide zigzag over the whole platter rather than serving it on the side. It reads as a finished dish.
recipes.garden: Nothing here needs a garden, which is exactly why this is the February recipe.
recipes.leftovers: Chickpeas soften; roast a fresh half batch if you care, or accept them soft in a wrap with the tahini.

recipes.title: Creamy Tomato Rigatoni with White Beans
recipes.blurb: The creaminess comes from blended cannellini beans, not cream — which also means 14 grams of protein and 9 grams of fiber a serving. Twenty-five minutes.
steps: Boil the pasta in well-salted water. Reserve 1 cup of pasta water.
Cook the onion in oil over medium 7 minutes; add garlic and pepper flakes 45 seconds; fry the tomato paste 60 seconds until dark.
Add crushed tomatoes and salt; simmer 8 minutes.
Blend the beans with 1/2 cup of the pasta water until completely smooth, then stir into the sauce. It goes from red to a glossy orange-pink — that is the cream you didn't add.
Add spinach and let it wilt, 2 minutes.
Toss the drained pasta into the sauce with a splash of pasta water. Off heat, add basil and parmesan.

omnivore.label: Add chicken sausage or shrimp
omnivore.note: Brown one link, sliced, and stir into individual bowls.
steps: Brown and slice the sausage; add to the omnivores' bowls with a spoon of extra sauce.

recipes.kidTweak: This is already the recipe most kids ask for again. If yours won't eat visible spinach, wilt it in and blend it with the beans — it disappears completely into the sauce.
recipes.restaurantTouch: Finish the pasta in the sauce for a full minute with pasta water, tossing hard. That emulsion is what makes restaurant pasta cling instead of sit in a puddle.
recipes.garden: Basil, always basil.
recipes.leftovers: Keeps 4 days. The sauce alone freezes well without the pasta.

recipes.title: Skillet Black Bean Enchiladas
recipes.blurb: All the flavor of rolled enchiladas with none of the rolling. One skillet, thirty minutes, and the kids can pile on their own toppings.
steps: Heat broiler position rack and set the oven to 400°F. Cook onion and pepper in oil 7 minutes.
Add garlic and spices, 45 seconds. Add beans, crushed tomatoes, salsa and corn; simmer 8 minutes until thick.
Fold in the tortilla strips so they are coated and submerged — they soften into layers, like a lazy lasagna.
Top with cheese and bake 12 minutes until bubbling; broil 90 seconds for browned spots if you want them.
Finish with cilantro, lime and dollops of yogurt. Avocado if you have one.

omnivore.label: Add shredded chicken
omnivore.note: A rotisserie chicken breast, shredded, stirred into half the skillet before baking.
steps: Stir shredded chicken into one half of the skillet before adding cheese, and remember which side is which.

recipes.kidTweak: Kids who dislike 'mixed' food eat this fine because it reads as nachos. Serve with extra tortillas.
recipes.restaurantTouch: Thin the yogurt with lime juice into a drizzle and squeeze it over in stripes rather than spooning it on.
recipes.garden: Peppers, tomatoes, cilantro — all September, all from the yard.
recipes.leftovers: Keeps 4 days, reheats in a skillet with a lid. Softer, still good.

recipes.title: Cold Peanut Noodles with Snap Peas and Edamame
recipes.blurb: Twenty minutes, no oven, and a peanut sauce that keeps a week in the fridge. The dinner for the night nobody wants to turn on the stove.
steps: Cook the noodles, drain, and rinse under cold water until completely cool. Toss with a teaspoon of sesame oil so they don't clump.

Whisk peanut butter, soy sauce, rice vinegar, maple, ginger, garlic, sriracha, the rest of the sesame oil and the juice of one lime. It will look broken — add warm water a tablespoon at a time until it is the texture of heavy cream.
Drop the snap peas into the noodle water for 45 seconds before you drain it, then straight into cold water. Bright green, still crunchy.
Toss noodles with three quarters of the sauce, then fold in all the vegetables and edamame.
Top with scallions, cilantro, pepitas, the remaining sauce and the second lime cut into wedges.

omnivore.label: Add poached or grilled chicken
omnivore.note: Cold sliced chicken folds in without changing anything else.
steps: Fold sliced cold chicken into the omnivores' portions with an extra spoon of sauce.

recipes.kidTweak: Serve a kid's portion before the sriracha goes in, sauce on the side. Peanut noodles are a top-three kid food when they control the sauce.
recipes.restaurantTouch: Julienne the carrots properly — long thin matchsticks, not shreds. Texture is the entire dish here.
recipes.garden: Snap peas in June, cucumbers and peppers in August; all of it works.
recipes.leftovers: Holds 3 days and travels well. This is the best lunchbox item in the collection.
recipes.allergenNote: Contains peanuts. Sunflower seed butter substitutes one-for-one for a nut-free school lunch.

recipes.title: Slow-Roasted Salmon with Lemon, Dill and Asparagus
recipes.blurb: Roasted at 275°F so it never dries out and never turns the kitchen fishy. This is the two-fish-a-week recipe, and it is genuinely easier than the fast version.

ingredients.prep: halved if small, quartered if large

steps: Heat oven to 425°F. Toss potatoes with 1 tbsp oil and salt, roast 25 minutes while you prep everything else.
Drop the oven to 275°F. Push the potatoes aside, lay the salmon on the pan, rub with 1 tbsp oil, season, and cover with lemon slices and garlic.
Roast 22-25 minutes. At 275°F the albumin never squeezes out, so the fish stays silky — it is done when it flakes at a gentle press, around 125°F internal.
Add the asparagus alongside for the last 12 minutes with the last tablespoon of oil.
Sauce: stir yogurt with dill, Dijon, lemon juice, salt and pepper.
Serve with the sauce spooned across and extra lemon.

vegetarianSwap.label: For the vegetarian at the table
vegetarianSwap.note: The same lemon-dill-garlic treatment on a tray of white beans and cherry tomatoes, roasted alongside for 20 minutes, gives the vegetarians at the table the identical plate without a separate dinner.
steps: Toss the beans and tomatoes with 1 tbsp olive oil, garlic, lemon slices and a pinch of salt in a small baking dish.
Roast alongside the salmon for 20 minutes until the tomatoes burst. Finish with the same dill-yogurt sauce.

recipes.kidTweak: Kids usually prefer salmon plain with lemon. Serve the sauce on the side and let them dip the potatoes in it.
recipes.restaurantTouch: Slow roasting is what high-end restaurants do to salmon. It is a lower oven and more time, and it is nearly impossible to overcook.
recipes.garden: Dill self-seeds and comes back every year once you let one plant flower.
recipes.leftovers: Cold salmon flaked over the next day's salad is better than reheating it.
recipes.heartNote: Two servings of fatty fish a week is a specific AHA recommendation for people with coronary heart disease. This recipe is one of them.

recipes.title: Garden Frittata
recipes.blurb: Breakfast for dinner, built on whatever the garden gave you. Extra whites keep it light without making it taste like a diet.
steps: Heat oven to 375°F. Beat eggs, whites, milk, salt and pepper until completely uniform — 30 seconds of real whisking, not ten stirs.
Cook the onion in oil in an oven-safe skillet over medium 6 minutes; add zucchini and cook 5 more until it browns at the edges.
Add garlic and spinach; cook until the spinach wilts and any water has evaporated. Wet vegetables make a weeping frittata.
Pour in the eggs, scatter the tomatoes and goat cheese, and cook undisturbed 3 minutes until the edges set.
Transfer to the oven for 12-14 minutes until the center is just barely set — it keeps cooking out of the oven.
Rest 5 minutes, then slide onto a board, top with basil, and cut into wedges. Serve with toast.

omnivore.label: Add crumbled chicken sausage
omnivore.note: Brown it with the onions if the whole pan can be non-vegetarian; otherwise scatter it on one half after the eggs go in.
steps: Brown the sausage, then scatter it over half the pan right after pouring in the eggs.

recipes.kidTweak: A frittata is just eggs. Serve a wedge with toast and fruit and most kids are happy.
recipes.restaurantTouch: Pull it from the oven while the center still wobbles slightly. Overcooked frittata is rubbery and everyone has eaten one.
recipes.garden: Precisely the recipe for a Tuesday in August when there are three zucchini on the counter.
recipes.leftovers: Excellent cold or at room temperature, which makes it a lunchbox and a picnic item too.

recipes.title: Lentil-Mushroom Shepherd's Pie
recipes.blurb: The Sunday dinner. A deeply savory lentil and mushroom base under a sweet potato and Yukon mash. Worth the hour, and it makes two dinners.
steps: Boil both potatoes in salted water until fork-tender, 15-18 minutes. Drain, return to the dry pot for 60 seconds to steam off, then mash with warm milk, butter, salt and pepper. Do not overwork it.
Meanwhile brown the mushrooms in 1 tbsp oil in a wide dutch oven over medium-high, undisturbed for 4 minutes, then tossing, until they have given up their water and browned. Remove.
Add the last tablespoon of oil, then onion, carrot and celery; cook 10 minutes. Add garlic and thyme, then fry the tomato paste 90 seconds.
Deglaze with the wine, scraping everything off the bottom, and let it reduce by half.

Add lentils, broth, soy sauce, the mushrooms and salt. Simmer 30-35 minutes until the lentils are tender and the mixture is thick — thicker than you think; it should mound on a spoon. Stir in the peas.
Spread the filling in a 9x13 dish, top with mash, rough up the surface with a fork so it catches color, and bake at 400°F for 25 minutes until the peaks brown.

omnivore.label: Add ground turkey or lamb
omnivore.note: Brown a half pound and fold it into half the filling before it goes into the dish.
steps: Brown the turkey with a pinch of thyme and fold it into one side of the filling. Mark that side.

recipes.kidTweak: The sweet potato mash does the persuading. Some kids want the mash and the filling served side by side instead of layered — fine.
recipes.restaurantTouch: The soy sauce is not a flavor you taste, it is the glutamate that makes a meatless braise taste like it has depth. Same job as an anchovy.
recipes.garden: Thyme, carrots, and fall potatoes.
recipes.leftovers: Better the second day. Assemble unbaked and freeze up to 3 months; bake from frozen at 375°F for 70 minutes covered, 15 uncovered.

recipes.title: Crispy Gnocchi with Brown Butter, Sage and White Beans
recipes.blurb: Skip the boiling water. Shelf-stable gnocchi dropped straight into a hot pan turns into little crisp-shelled pillows, and brown butter with fried sage is the sauce that ruins you for other sauces.
steps: Heat the olive oil in a large skillet over medium-high. Add the gnocchi straight from the package — do not boil them — in one layer. Leave them alone for 4 minutes. Do not stir, do not check. That undisturbed contact is the entire recipe.
Toss once and cook 3-4 minutes more until most sides are golden and the insides have gone tender. Tip them onto a plate.

Turn the heat to medium and add the butter. It will foam, then quiet, then the milk solids at the bottom will turn the color of a hazelnut and it will smell like toffee — about 3 minutes. Watch it. Brown butter goes from perfect to burnt in fifteen seconds.
Drop in the sage leaves; they will crackle and crisp in about 30 seconds. Add the sliced garlic and cook 30 seconds more, no longer, or it turns bitter.
Add the beans and spinach with the salt and pepper. Toss until the spinach collapses, 1-2 minutes.
Return the gnocchi, add the lemon zest and juice, and toss once. The acid is what keeps all that butter from sitting heavy. Finish with walnuts and parmesan.

omnivore.label: Add crumbled Italian chicken sausage
omnivore.note: Brown it first in the same skillet, lift it out, then start the gnocchi in the fat it leaves behind. Two minutes of extra work, and the vegetarian version is still the one everyone reaches for.
steps: Brown the sausage over medium-high, breaking it up, 5-6 minutes. Lift it out with a slotted spoon and set it aside.
Crisp the gnocchi in the rendered fat, and scatter the sausage over the omnivores' bowls at the end.

recipes.kidTweak: Serve their portion before the lemon goes in — some kids read acid as 'sour' rather than 'bright'. The crisp gnocchi and fried sage leaves usually do the convincing on their own.
recipes.restaurantTouch: Fry a few extra sage leaves and lay them whole across the top. They shatter like a chip and they are the first thing anyone photographs.
recipes.garden: Sage is a perennial in zone 6a and one of the easiest herbs you will ever grow — one plant by the back door survives Ohio winters and gives you leaves for this from April to November.
recipes.leftovers: Eat it the night you make it. Crisp gnocchi go soft in the fridge and no amount of reheating brings the shell back.
recipes.heartNote: Scores low mostly on sodium — shelf-stable gnocchi carries about 430 mg per 100 g before you add anything, and that is roughly two-thirds of the 808 mg in a serving. The rest of the plate is doing real work: 10.6 g of fiber from the beans, spinach and walnuts is more than most dinners here. Salt the pan lightly and the score moves.

recipes.title: Real French Onion Soup
recipes.blurb: Five pounds of onions cooked down for the better part of an hour into something jammy and almost sweet, under a raft of bread and melted Gruyère. There is no shortcut and there does not need to be — the stove does the work while you do something else.
equipment: oven-safe bowls or a sheet pan
steps: Melt the butter with the oil in a dutch oven over medium. Add all the onions with the salt and sugar. They will look like far too many. They will cook down to a quarter of that.

Cook 45-55 minutes, stirring every 5-8 minutes and scraping the brown film off the bottom each time. That film is the flavor. If the pan looks dry and dark, add a splash of water and scrape. Do not raise the heat to hurry it — you get burnt edges and raw centers.
When the onions are deep amber and jammy, add the garlic and cook 1 minute. Stir in the flour and cook 2 minutes to lose the raw taste.
Pour in the wine and scrape the bottom clean. Simmer until it is nearly gone, about 4 minutes.
Add the broth, soy sauce, thyme sprigs and bay leaves. The soy is not a flavor you will taste — it is doing the savory work beef broth normally does. Simmer 20 minutes.
Fish out the thyme stems and bay. Stir in the balsamic and pepper, then taste. It should make you want another spoonful immediately; if it does not, it needs salt or another splash of vinegar.

Toast the baguette slices. Ladle soup into oven-safe bowls, float two slices on each, pile on the Gruyère, and broil 2-3 minutes until the cheese is bubbling and blistered in spots. Let them sit 2 minutes — molten cheese is a real burn risk.
recipes.kidTweak: Serve theirs in a regular bowl with the cheese toast on the side, unbroiled. The bowl-under-a-broiler part is the fun of it, but it comes out at 400°F.
recipes.restaurantTouch: Grate the Gruyère yourself and let a little fall down the outside of the bowl. It bakes onto the rim and you get a crisp cheese edge, which is the best bite in the whole dish.
recipes.garden: Onions and thyme both come out of a small bed easily. Six storage onions from an August harvest is a single row — and this soup is what storage onions are for in February.
recipes.leftovers: The soup base keeps 5 days refrigerated and 3 months frozen, and genuinely improves overnight. Toast and broil fresh bread each time; a soggy raft reheated is a sad thing.
recipes.prepAhead: Caramelize the onions on a Sunday and refrigerate them. Soup on a Wednesday is then 25 minutes.
recipes.heartNote: This is the lowest-scoring recipe in the collection and it is not a mistake. A serving carries about 853 mg of sodium and 9.5 g of saturated fat, almost all of it from broth, baguette and an ounce of Gruyère. Low-sodium broth cuts roughly 300 mg. It is a February Sunday dish, not a Tuesday one, and the app is not going to pretend otherwise.

recipes.title: Chile Crisp Noodles with Jammy Eggs
recipes.blurb: Fifteen minutes, one pot, and a bowl of noodles slick with chili crisp and soy that tastes like something you would order out. The jammy egg on top is not optional in the way that things labeled optional usually are.
steps: Bring a large pot of water to a boil. Lower the eggs in on a spoon and set a timer for 7 minutes exactly — that is the window for a set white and a center that is still liquid gold. Lift them into cold water when the timer goes.
In the same water, cook the noodles to just under the package time. Add the bok choy for the last 90 seconds. Save half a cup of the cooking water, then drain.

While that happens, whisk the chili crisp, soy, vinegar, sesame oil, maple and grated garlic in the bottom of a big bowl. Spoon the chili crisp from the bottom of the jar, not the oil off the top — the crunchy sediment is what you are paying for.
Tip the hot noodles and bok choy straight into the bowl and toss hard, adding splashes of the reserved water until the sauce coats every strand rather than pooling at the bottom.
Peel the eggs and halve them. Pile noodles into bowls, set the egg halves on top cut side up, and finish with scallions, peanuts and sesame seeds.

omnivore.label: Add poached shrimp
omnivore.note: They cook in the same pot in the same three minutes, so this genuinely costs nothing extra in time or dishes.
steps: After lifting out the eggs, drop the shrimp into the same water for 2-3 minutes until they curl and turn opaque. Lift them out before the noodles go in.

recipes.kidTweak: Pull out a portion of plain noodles with a little sesame oil and soy before the chili crisp goes anywhere near the bowl. Add a jammy egg and they have the same dinner, minus the heat.
recipes.restaurantTouch: Warm the chili crisp and soy mixture for 20 seconds in the microwave before tossing. Warm sauce clings; cold sauce slides off and puddles.
recipes.garden: Scallions regrow from the root ends in a jar of water on the windowsill, indefinitely, for free. Bok choy is a fast spring and fall crop — 45 days from seed.
recipes.leftovers: Noodles keep 3 days but the peanuts go soft. Store the crunchy toppings separately and re-crisp the noodles in a hot dry skillet rather than a microwave.

recipes.title: Mushroom Bourguignon
recipes.blurb: The braise that makes people go quiet at the table. Mushrooms browned hard, red wine reduced properly, and dried porcini doing the job that beef normally does. It tastes like it took all day and takes about an hour.
steps: Cover the dried porcini with the hot broth and leave them to soak. This is your stock, and it is the reason this tastes like a braise rather than a mushroom stew.

Heat the oil in a dutch oven over high until it shimmers. Add half the fresh mushrooms in one layer, salt them lightly, and leave them for 4 minutes without touching. Toss, cook 3 more, and remove. Repeat with the rest. Crowding the pan steams them and you lose the whole dish here.
Lower to medium and melt the butter. Add onion and carrot with a pinch of salt, cook 8 minutes until softening and browning at the edges.
Add the garlic and tomato paste and cook 2 minutes, stirring, until the paste darkens from red to brick. Sprinkle over the flour and cook another minute.
Pour in the wine and scrape every brown patch off the bottom. Simmer hard 5 minutes until it has reduced by about a third and no longer smells sharp.

Lift the porcini out of the broth, chop them, and add them to the pot. Pour in the soaking broth, leaving the last tablespoon of grit behind in the bowl. Add thyme, bay, soy sauce, the browned mushrooms, salt and pepper.
Simmer uncovered 25-30 minutes until the sauce coats a spoon. Meanwhile boil the potatoes in salted water until a knife slides in, then mash with the warm milk and a good pinch of salt.
Pull the thyme stems and bay. Taste for salt — a braise this dark usually wants a little more than you expect. Spoon over the mash and shower with parsley.

omnivore.label: Add seared sirloin
omnivore.note: Sear it in the pot first and it leaves a fond the mushrooms then build on, which improves the vegetarian version too. Add the meat back only to the omnivores' plates.
steps: Pat the beef dry, salt it, and sear in the hot oil 4-5 minutes until well browned on two sides. Remove and set aside.
Return it to the pot for the last 10 minutes of simmering, or warm it separately and spoon it over individual plates.

recipes.kidTweak: Mushrooms cut small disappear into the sauce; cut large they are a texture some kids will not accept. Chop a portion of the mushrooms finely before browning and serve that side of the pot to them, over plenty of mash.
recipes.restaurantTouch: Take the pot off the heat and swirl in one final tablespoon of cold butter until it disappears. That is a French finish called monter au beurre and it is the difference between a good sauce and a glossy one.
recipes.garden: Carrots, thyme and parsley all come out of a few square feet. Thyme in particular is a plant-once perennial that survives Ohio winters under a little mulch.
recipes.leftovers: Better on day two, genuinely. Keeps 4 days refrigerated and 3 months frozen. Freeze the braise alone; mashed potatoes turn grainy after thawing.
recipes.prepAhead: Make the braise a day ahead and reheat gently. Mash the potatoes fresh — it is 20 minutes and it matters.

recipes.title: Baked Feta Pasta with Blistered Tomatoes
recipes.blurb: A block of feta in a dish of cherry tomatoes and olive oil, roasted until the tomatoes burst and the cheese slumps, then stirred into a sauce. It went round the world for a reason, and it is genuinely good.
steps: Heat the oven to 400°F. Tip the tomatoes and whole garlic cloves into a baking dish, pour over 3 tablespoons of the oil, and toss with the pepper flakes, oregano, salt and pepper.
Clear a well in the middle, set the block of feta in it, and pour the last tablespoon of oil over the cheese.

Roast 35 minutes, until the tomatoes have collapsed and split and the feta is soft and browning at the corners. If the top is still pale, give it 3 minutes under the broiler — those browned edges are most of the flavor.
Boil the pasta in well-salted water to just under package time. Save a cup of the water before draining.
Mash everything in the baking dish together with a fork. The garlic cloves will have gone sweet and will smash to nothing. Stir in the spinach while the dish is still hot so it wilts.
Add the pasta and enough cooking water to loosen it into a sauce that clings. Finish with lemon juice and torn basil off the heat.

omnivore.label: Add roasted shrimp
omnivore.note: They go into the same dish for the last 6 minutes, so there is no second pan.
steps: Scatter the shrimp around the edges of the baking dish for the final 6 minutes of roasting, until pink and opaque. Lift them out before mashing if you want to keep the base vegetarian, and add them to individual bowls.

recipes.kidTweak: This is one of the easier sells in the whole book — it reads as cheesy pasta. Leave out the pepper flakes and stir a spoonful of the sauce through their portion before adding the spinach.
recipes.restaurantTouch: Reserve a handful of the roasted tomatoes before mashing and spoon them whole over the top. Whole blistered tomatoes still burst in the mouth; mashed ones do not.
recipes.garden: This is the August recipe for a cherry tomato plant that has gotten away from you. Sungold and Black Cherry both roast beautifully and one plant will supply this all summer.
recipes.leftovers: Keeps 3 days. It tightens up in the fridge — reheat with a splash of water in a skillet rather than dry in the microwave.
recipes.heartNote: The 8 oz of feta is the whole score: 8.4 g saturated fat and most of the 549 mg sodium per serving. It is still under the 700 mg the AHA flags for a single meal, and dropping to 6 oz of feta with an extra pint of tomatoes changes the dish very little.

recipes.title: Crispy Rice Bowl with Kimchi and a Fried Egg
recipes.blurb: Cold leftover rice pressed into a hot pan and left there until the bottom forms a golden crust you have to break with a spoon. Kimchi, a runny egg, and that crust — it is the best thing you can do with yesterday's rice.
steps: Use cold rice. Freshly cooked rice is too wet and will steam into mush instead of crisping — this is the one non-negotiable in the recipe.
Whisk the gochujang, soy, maple and 2 tablespoons of the kimchi juice together and set it aside.

Heat 1 tablespoon of the canola oil in a large skillet over medium-high. Add the kimchi and garlic and fry 3 minutes until the edges darken and it smells sweet rather than sharp. Push it to one side, add the spinach, and toss until it wilts. Scrape it all onto a plate.

Add the remaining oil and the sesame oil. Add the rice and press it into a flat, even layer with the back of a spatula. Now leave it for 5-6 minutes. No stirring. You will hear it crackle and you should let it keep crackling.
Lift an edge with the spatula. When the underside is deep golden and lifts in a sheet, break it into rough pieces and toss with the sauce and the kimchi mixture.
Fry the eggs in a separate pan in a film of oil over medium-high, spooning hot oil over the whites until the edges are lacy and brown but the yolk is still liquid, about 2 minutes.
Pile the rice into bowls, set an egg on each, and top with scallions, sesame seeds and cold cucumber slices. Break the yolk into the rice at the table.

omnivore.label: Add sliced pork tenderloin
omnivore.note: Sear it first and rest it while the rice crisps; slice it thin across the grain over the omnivores' bowls.
steps: Season the tenderloin with salt and sear in the skillet over medium-high, turning, 12-14 minutes until 145°F at the center. Rest 5 minutes before slicing thin.

recipes.kidTweak: Kimchi is a hard sell for a lot of kids. Crisp their rice plain with a little sesame oil and soy, top with a fried egg, and give them the cucumbers on the side — the crust is the part they will actually care about.
recipes.restaurantTouch: Serve it in a shallow bowl and lay the egg slightly off-center so the yolk runs toward one side. Add one extra spoonful of kimchi juice around the edge; it pools and looks like a sauce because it is one.
recipes.garden: Napa cabbage for homemade kimchi is a straightforward fall crop in Ohio, sown in August and harvested after the first light frosts, which sweeten it.
recipes.leftovers: The crisp does not survive storage. Make only what you will eat, and use tomorrow's rice for tomorrow's version.
recipes.heartNote: A whole egg per person puts this at 186 mg of cholesterol a serving. Saturated fat is genuinely low at 2.8 g, and kimchi contributes fermented fiber. Use two eggs across four bowls, split, and the score jumps.

recipes.title: Mushroom Birria Tacos with Consommé
recipes.blurb: Tortillas dipped in a deep red chile broth, griddled until the edges go crisp, and served with a cup of that same broth for dunking. It is a whole event, and the broth is what people remember.
steps: Toast the dried chiles in a dry skillet over medium, 30-40 seconds a side, until they smell sweet and smoky. Do not let them blacken — burnt chile turns the whole pot bitter and there is no fixing it.
Cover the chiles with 2 cups of the broth and simmer 10 minutes until soft.

Blend the softened chiles and their liquid with the tomatoes, quartered onion, garlic, chipotles, cumin, oregano, cinnamon and vinegar until completely smooth. Push it through a sieve if you want a glossy consommé; skip that and it is rustic.

Heat the oil in a dutch oven over medium-high. Brown the portobello strips hard, 6-8 minutes, in two batches — this is where the meaty texture comes from. Add the shredded jackfruit and cook 3 minutes more.
Pour in the blended chile sauce and the remaining 3 cups of broth. Add the salt and simmer 30 minutes until the broth is deep red and tastes round rather than sharp.
Lift the solids out with a slotted spoon into a bowl. Keep the broth at a bare simmer — that is your consommé.

Dip a tortilla into the red broth so both sides are stained, lay it on a hot griddle, scatter cheese on half, add the filling, and fold. Griddle 2 minutes a side until the cheese has melted and the edges are crisp and lacquered.
Serve with small bowls of the hot consommé, plus red onion, cilantro and lime.

omnivore.label: Add braised chicken thighs
omnivore.note: They braise in the same pot in the same chile broth, so the two versions taste like the same dish rather than two different dinners.
steps: Brown the thighs before the mushrooms and set them aside. Return them to the pot with the chile sauce and simmer 30 minutes, then shred with two forks and keep them in a separate bowl from the mushroom filling.

recipes.kidTweak: Guajillos are mild — the heat here is mostly the chipotles. Leave those out entirely and the broth is sweet and smoky rather than spicy. Most kids treat these as red quesadillas, which is fine.
recipes.restaurantTouch: Skim the red-orange fat off the top of the broth and brush it onto the tortillas before griddling. That lacquered shine is the whole visual identity of this dish.
recipes.garden: Roma tomatoes, cilantro and onions all grow well here. Cilantro bolts in July heat — sow it in April and again in late August rather than fighting the middle of summer.
recipes.leftovers: Filling and consommé both keep 4 days and freeze 3 months. Assemble and griddle fresh; a pre-made taco reheated goes soft.
recipes.prepAhead: Make the filling and broth a day ahead. Assembly is then 15 minutes, which makes this genuinely workable for a crowd.

recipes.title: Skillet Paneer Tikka Masala
recipes.blurb: Cubes of paneer browned in butter and folded into a tomato sauce built on bloomed garam masala. Restaurant tikka masala usually runs on a cup of cream; this one uses three tablespoons and gets the rest of its body from blended onion.
steps: Start the rice. Pat the paneer cubes dry — wet paneer will not brown, it will squeak.

Melt 1 tablespoon of the butter with the oil in a large skillet over medium-high. Brown the paneer on two or three sides, about 5 minutes total, and lift it out. It should be golden and slightly crisp; it will soften again in the sauce.
Add the onion to the same pan and cook 8 minutes until soft and browning. Add the garlic and ginger and cook 1 minute.

Add the remaining butter, then all the ground spices, and stir constantly for 60 seconds. Blooming them in fat rather than dumping them into liquid is the single biggest difference between this and a flat curry.
Stir in the tomato paste and cook 2 minutes until it darkens. Add the crushed tomatoes and broth, scrape the bottom, and simmer 12 minutes.
Blend the sauce smooth — an immersion blender in the pan is easiest. This is what gives it the silky body that would otherwise take a cup of cream.
Stir in the cream, salt and peas, return the paneer, and simmer 4 minutes more. Finish with lemon juice off the heat and a heap of cilantro. Serve over the rice.

omnivore.label: Add chicken thigh
omnivore.note: Brown it in the same pan before the paneer and add it back with the peas. The sauce was designed to take either.
steps: Season and brown the chicken over medium-high, 6-7 minutes. Set aside and return it to the sauce for the final 8 minutes of simmering, until cooked through.

recipes.kidTweak: Leave the pepper flakes out and this is mild — garam masala is aromatic, not hot. Paneer holds its shape and does not string, which makes it an easier cheese for a suspicious kid than melted mozzarella.
recipes.restaurantTouch: Swirl the last spoonful of cream over the top in a spiral rather than stirring it in, and drop the cilantro on at the very last second. Both things happen at the pass in a restaurant for exactly this reason.
recipes.garden: Cilantro and hot peppers both do well here. Ginger will grow in a pot on a sunny porch through an Ohio summer and gives you tender young rhizomes in October.
recipes.leftovers: Keeps 4 days and freezes 2 months, though the paneer firms up after freezing. Reheat gently — a hard boil makes the cream break.
recipes.prepAhead: The sauce keeps 4 days on its own. Brown fresh paneer and fold it in and dinner is 10 minutes.

recipes.title: Sticky Gochujang Tofu
recipes.blurb: Tofu cornstarched and fried until the outside shatters, then tossed in a glaze that reduces to a lacquer in the pan. Cold cucumber salad on the side because something has to cut through it.
steps: Start the rice. Press the tofu between paper towels under something heavy for 15 minutes — every minute of pressing is a degree of crispness later.
Toss the cucumber slices with the salt and 1 tablespoon of the rice vinegar and leave them in a bowl. They will weep and turn snappy while you cook.
Toss the tofu cubes in the cornstarch until every face is dusted and dry-looking.
Heat the canola oil in a large nonstick skillet over medium-high. Add the tofu in one layer and fry 3-4 minutes a side, turning twice, until deep golden and audibly crisp. Move it to a plate.
Whisk the gochujang, soy, maple, remaining vinegar, sesame oil, garlic and ginger. Pour it into the hot pan and let it bubble 60-90 seconds — it will thicken and go glossy.
Kill the heat, return the tofu, and toss fast. Sauce added to a hot pan glazes; sauce added to a cool pan just soaks in and the crisp is gone.
Serve over rice with the drained cucumbers, scallions and sesame seeds.

omnivore.label: Glaze chicken thighs the same way
omnivore.note: The glaze works identically on chicken. Cook them in a second skillet and both halves of the table eat the same dinner.
steps: Sear the thighs 6-7 minutes a side over medium until 165°F, then toss with half the glaze in the pan off the heat.

recipes.kidTweak: Gochujang is sweet-savory more than hot, but it does carry heat. Pull out a few tofu cubes after frying and toss them in soy sauce and maple alone — same crunch, no chile.
recipes.restaurantTouch: Save one tablespoon of the glaze and brush it over the plated tofu with the back of a spoon. It sets into a shine that tossing alone will not give you.
recipes.garden: Cucumbers are among the easiest and highest-yielding things in an Ohio garden — one hill of a pickling variety supplies this all July.
recipes.leftovers: The tofu softens overnight. Reheat in a dry skillet over medium-high for 3 minutes and most of the crust comes back; the microwave will not do it.

recipes.title: Harissa Butter Chickpeas over Garlic Yogurt
recipes.blurb: Chickpeas crisped in harissa butter, spooned over a pool of cold garlicky yogurt so it streaks pink where the two meet. Twenty minutes, mostly pantry, and it looks like something you would pay for.
steps: Stir the yogurt with the grated garlic clove, half the lemon juice, the zest and a quarter teaspoon of the salt. Spread it across the bottom of a wide shallow bowl or four plates and put it in the fridge. Cold yogurt under hot chickpeas is the whole trick.
Dry the chickpeas properly on a towel. Wet chickpeas steam and stay soft; dry ones blister.
Heat the olive oil in a skillet over medium-high and add the chickpeas in one layer. Cook 6-8 minutes, shaking occasionally, until they are browned in patches and some have split.
Lower the heat to medium. Add the butter, sliced garlic, harissa, cumin and paprika. Stir for 2 minutes as the butter foams and the spices bloom into it — the whole pan should go rust-colored.
Add the spinach and the remaining salt and toss until it wilts, about a minute.
Spoon the hot chickpeas straight onto the cold yogurt without stirring. Finish with the rest of the lemon juice, the mint and pistachios. Serve with warm pita to drag through it.
recipes.kidTweak: Harissa is properly hot. Set aside a portion of chickpeas after they crisp and before the harissa goes in, toss those with butter and a shake of paprika, and give them the yogurt on the side rather than underneath.
recipes.restaurantTouch: Spread the yogurt with the back of a spoon in one sweeping curve so it has a lip at the edge. Everything after that lands in a pool, and the plate looks composed rather than dumped.
recipes.garden: Mint will take over a bed if you let it — grow it in a buried pot. Spinach is a cool-season crop here, sown in early April and again in September.
recipes.leftovers: Store the chickpeas and yogurt separately, 3 days. Re-crisp the chickpeas in a dry skillet; do not microwave them into the yogurt.

recipes.title: Cacio e Pepe with Sweet Peas
recipes.blurb: Four ingredients and a technique. Pecorino, black pepper toasted in a dry pan, and starchy pasta water whisked into a sauce that clings like cream without any cream in it. Peas make it dinner rather than a side.
steps: Boil the pasta in less water than usual, salted, so the water gets genuinely starchy. That water is an ingredient, not waste.
Grate the cheese on the finest holes you have while the water heats. Pre-grated cheese is coated in anti-caking starch and will go grainy on you — this is the most common way this dish fails.
Toast the cracked pepper in a dry skillet over medium for 60 seconds, until it smells sharp and floral. Add the butter and let it melt.
Add the peas and a ladle of pasta water to the skillet and simmer 2 minutes.
Drain the pasta about 2 minutes shy of package time, reserving 1.5 cups of water. Add the pasta to the skillet with another ladle of water and toss over low heat for a minute.

Take the pan off the heat and wait 30 seconds. Now add the cheese in three handfuls, tossing hard between each, adding splashes of water as you go. Off the heat is essential — direct heat is what makes the cheese seize into strings.
Keep tossing until it turns glossy and coats the pasta. Serve immediately with lemon zest if you want it, in warmed bowls. This dish waits for nobody.
recipes.kidTweak: Halve the pepper. This is macaroni and cheese with a better pedigree and it usually lands well, though the peas may get picked out — put them in anyway.
recipes.restaurantTouch: Warm the bowls under hot tap water and dry them. Cacio e pepe on a cold plate tightens within a minute; on a warm one it stays silky to the last bite.
recipes.garden: Sugar snap and shelling peas go in the ground here in late March, as early as you can work the soil, and are done by late June. Fresh shelled peas in this in May are worth the row.
recipes.leftovers: Almost none, in practice. What survives will not reheat well — the emulsion breaks. Make what you will eat.
recipes.heartNote: Pecorino is one of the saltiest cheeses there is — the 977 mg of sodium and 11.8 g of saturated fat here are essentially all cheese. That is what the dish is. Swapping a third of the pecorino for parmesan drops the sodium by about a quarter without losing the emulsion. Treat it as a small plate rather than a weekly dinner if sodium is something you are watching.

recipes.title: Charred Cabbage Steaks with Miso Butter
recipes.blurb: A three-dollar head of cabbage roasted hard until the outer leaves blacken and the inside goes sweet and silky, then brushed with miso butter. It is the cheapest thing in this collection and one of the best.

ingredients.prep: cut in 1.5-inch wedges through the core

steps: Heat the oven to 450°F with a sheet pan already inside. A screaming hot pan is what gives you a charred face rather than a steamed one.
Cut the cabbage into wedges through the core so each one holds together. Brush both cut faces with the canola oil and salt them.
Lay the wedges on the hot pan — they should hiss — and roast 20 minutes without turning.
Meanwhile mash the butter with the miso, maple, rice vinegar and grated garlic until smooth.
Flip the wedges and roast 12-15 minutes more, until the edges are properly blackened in places. Do not rescue them early; charred is the point and the blackened leaves taste of caramel, not ash.
Cook the rice, and boil the edamame 4 minutes, then toss it with the sesame oil.
Brush the hot cabbage generously with the miso butter so it melts into the layers. Top with scallions and sesame seeds and serve over rice with the edamame.

omnivore.label: Add roasted salmon
omnivore.note: It roasts on the same pan for the last 12 minutes, and the miso butter is just as good on fish as it is on cabbage.
steps: Add the salmon to the pan when you flip the cabbage. Roast 12-14 minutes until it flakes, and brush it with the miso butter too.

recipes.kidTweak: Charred cabbage is a hard first sell. Pull two wedges before they blacken, at the 20-minute mark, and brush them with butter and maple only — sweeter, softer, no miso funk.
recipes.restaurantTouch: Spoon the extra miso butter into a small dish at the table and let people add more. Compound butter melting on the plate in front of someone does something no pre-sauced version can.
recipes.garden: Cabbage is one of the great value crops for a Northeast Ohio garden — a fall planting stands through frost, which makes it sweeter, and it stores for weeks.
recipes.leftovers: Keeps 3 days. Chop the leftovers and fry them hard in a skillet with the rice for a very good second dinner.
